A trained network and its sampling procedure are separate parts of a generative model.
A deterministic computation can produce a random output distribution when its input is random.

## Distinguish physical and generative time {#objects}

Let $o_t$ denote the observation available at robot time $t$.
A demonstrated action chunk is $A=(a_t,\ldots,a_{t+H-1})$, with $H$ future control steps.
If each action has $d_a$ coordinates, the chunk belongs to $\mathbb R^{H\times d_a}$.
Norms below compare all entries, or equivalently a flattened chunk.

| Symbol | Object |
|---|---|
| $A$ | A clean demonstrated action chunk used as a training target. |
| $\hat A$ | A predicted clean chunk. |
| $\epsilon$ | A Gaussian noise sample shaped like a chunk. |
| $A_k$ | An intermediate noisy chunk at diffusion index $k$. |
| $A^\tau$ | An intermediate chunk at flow time $\tau$. |
| $\theta$ | Learned parameters, fixed during ordinary inference. |

Robot time orders executed commands.
Diffusion index and flow time order computations that generate a chunk.
An intermediate noisy chunk is a numerical state inside the sampler; it is not the action currently being executed by the robot.

## Deterministic computation and random outputs {#randomness}

A deterministic generator can be written as $\hat A=G_\theta(o,z)$.
Fixing the observation, initial noise $z$, parameters, and numerical procedure fixes its output in an ideal deterministic implementation.
Sampling a different $z$ can produce a different output.

For a simple mathematical example, let $z\sim\mathcal N(0,1)$ and define

$$
  G(z)=
  \begin{cases}
  -2,&z<0,\\
  +2,&z\geq0.
  \end{cases}
$$

This deterministic function generates two equally likely values because its input is random.
It illustrates randomness propagation, not a proposed smooth flow model.

ODE flow sampling and DDIM with its stochasticity parameter set to zero can be deterministic conditional on their initial noise.
Other diffusion samplers inject additional noise during reverse steps, so fixing only the initial sample is insufficient.
[DDIM, Section 4](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.02502) distinguishes its deterministic case from the wider sampling family.

Reusing the same initial noise on every call, with deterministic sampling, chooses one repeatable mapping from observations to chunks.
Seeding a random-number generator once instead produces a reproducible sequence of draws; successive calls can still receive different noise.
It does not prove that the learned model has only one possible mode.
It also does not guarantee compatible chunks when the observation changes between replanning steps.

## Generation and execution are different stages {#execution}

A noisy intermediate sample belongs to the generator's computation.
Only a final prediction is considered for execution, and an [execution horizon](../physics/action-horizons.qmd#horizons) determines which commands are adopted before an update.
Reusing noise can make a deterministic sampler repeatable, but it does not ensure compatible chunks as observations change.
The [action-horizon note](../physics/action-horizons.qmd#execution) explains why switching between valid chunks requires its own mechanism.
Compare the [diffusion](diffusion.qmd) and [flow-matching](flow-matching.qmd) training targets before interpreting a paper's sampler.
